title: Writing Longer Pieces
description: How to plan, build, revise and finish an essay or report: the question, the thesis, structure, paragraphs, evidence, objections, revision, and the numbers and layout of a report.
audience: A capable adult who writes sentences and short paragraphs well and wants to sustain an argument over several pages. They have read the English course on reading, writing and rhetoric. Taking Reading and Research first is useful but not required.
outcomes: You'll be able to state a piece's reader, question and thesis.
You'll be able to order sections for an essay and for a decision report.
You'll be able to write paragraphs that each make one claim and explain their evidence.
You'll be able to state the strongest objection and qualify your claim.
You'll be able to revise from argument down to sentence and plan the work backwards from a deadline.
You'll be able to present numbers in a report so that text, table and figure agree.

modules.title: Plan the piece
modules.summary: Know the reader and the question, turn a topic into a claim worth arguing, and choose a structure before drafting.

modules.title: Build it
modules.summary: Paragraphs that each do one job, evidence that is explained, objections that are answered, and ways in and out that connect.

modules.title: Revise it
modules.summary: Revise from the whole to the sentence, cut what does not work, and run a process that finishes on time.

modules.title: Reports
modules.summary: Put the answer first, shape a report for scanning, and present numbers so that the text matches them.

lessons.title: Reader, purpose and form
lessons.objective: State a piece's reader, question and form, and set a word budget.

concepts.title: Purpose
concepts.summary: What the piece is meant to make its reader know, believe or do.

concepts.title: Form
concepts.summary: The kind of piece, such as an argumentative essay or a decision report, which sets the reader's expectations.

concepts.title: Word budget
concepts.summary: A plan for how many words each part of the piece gets.

misconceptions: Writing to show everything you know rather than to answer the reader's question.
Treating an essay and a report as the same thing in different clothes.
Starting to write without a length plan and running out of room for the argument.
sequence: Compare two pieces on the same topic, one for a tutor who asks 'what do you think and why?' and one for a manager who asks 'what should we do?'.
Name the reader, the question and the answer you want them to take away.
Distinguish an essay (a line of argument) from a report (a finding for a decision).
Set a word budget from the total.
Check that the budget fits the question.
examples: A 3,000-word essay: introduction 10% = 300 words, conclusion 10% = 300 words, body 80% = 2,400 words. Four body sections of equal size get 600 words each.

figures.shows: A planning grid with rows for reader, question, answer, form and length.
figures.learnerAction: Fill in each row for two example briefs.

questionPlan.sample: A 3,000-word essay has 10% for the introduction and 10% for the conclusion. How many words are left for the body?
Four equal body sections share those words. How long is each?
'Recommend whether we should switch suppliers' is the brief for:
questionPlan.answer: A report

lessons.title: From topic to thesis
lessons.objective: Turn a topic into a question and an arguable thesis, and test it for specificity and significance.

concepts.title: Topic
concepts.summary: A subject area, such as street trees.

concepts.title: Research or guiding question
concepts.summary: A question about the topic that the piece will answer.

concepts.title: Thesis
concepts.summary: A one-or-two sentence answer to the question that can be argued with evidence.

misconceptions: Offering a topic or a fact as a thesis.
Writing a thesis nobody could disagree with.
Writing a thesis too large for the length.
sequence: Move from the topic 'street trees' to a question: 'Do street trees reduce heat illness?'
Draft an answer and test it: could a reasonable person disagree? is it specific? does it say why it matters?
Compare a weak thesis with a strong one.
Check that the thesis fits the word budget.
Keep the thesis open to revision as the draft develops.
examples: Topic: street trees. Weak thesis: 'Street trees are important.' Stronger: 'Because shaded streets stay several degrees cooler in summer, cities with hot climates should plant street trees before building new cooling centres.'

figures.shows: A column of statements (topic, fact, question, thesis).

questionPlan.sample: Which is the strongest thesis?
questionPlan.answer: Cities in hot climates should plant street trees before building cooling centres, because shade lowers street temperatures
choices: Street trees exist in many cities
Cities in hot climates should plant street trees before building cooling centres, because shade lowers street temperatures

questionPlan.sample: 'Street trees are important' is weak because it:
questionPlan.answer: Could not be disagreed with and says nothing specific
choices: Could not be disagreed with and says nothing specific

questionPlan.sample: 'Street trees provide shade' is best described as:
questionPlan.answer: A fact, not a thesis

lessons.title: Structure and outline
lessons.objective: Order the parts of an essay and a report and choose an order that serves the reader.

concepts.title: Outline
concepts.summary: A plan of the piece's sections and the point each makes.

concepts.title: Answer first
concepts.summary: Opening with the conclusion and then supporting it, so a reader who stops early still has the answer.

concepts.title: Order of claims
concepts.summary: Arranging the points by logic, time, importance or a chain of cause.

misconceptions: Ordering by the order in which you found things out.
Putting the strongest point in the middle without a reason.
Using the five-paragraph shape for everything.
sequence: Draft an outline of an argumentative essay: introduction with thesis, reasons in order, objection and reply, conclusion.
Redraw it as a report with the answer first: summary, background, findings, options, recommendation.
Decide the order of reasons: by strength, by dependence, or by time.
Write one sentence per section.
Check each section answers the question.
examples: Essay order: introduction and thesis; reason 1; reason 2; objection and reply; conclusion. Report order: summary and recommendation; background; findings; options; next steps.

figures.learnerAction: Put them in a workable order.

questionPlan.sample: Order: Conclusion; Objection and reply; Introduction with thesis; Reason 1; Reason 2.
questionPlan.answer: Introduction with thesis, Reason 1, Reason 2, Objection and reply, Conclusion

questionPlan.sample: For a busy manager who may read only the first page, a report should:
questionPlan.answer: Put the recommendation first
choices: Build to the recommendation at the end

questionPlan.sample: Reasons that depend on one another are best ordered:
questionPlan.answer: So that each prepares the next
choices: So that each prepares the next

historyNotes: Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle (answer first) is the source of the answer-first habit in business writing; verify the date before citing.

lessons.title: Paragraphs that do one job
lessons.objective: Write a topic sentence that makes a claim, and cut or move a sentence that breaks a paragraph's unity.

concepts.title: Topic sentence
concepts.summary: A sentence, usually first, that states the paragraph's one claim.

concepts.title: Unity
concepts.summary: Every sentence in the paragraph supports its one claim.

concepts.title: Coherence
concepts.summary: The sentences follow each other so that a reader can see how they connect.

misconceptions: Starting a paragraph with a fact or a quotation and no claim.
Packing two claims into one paragraph.
Judging paragraph length by line count rather than by the idea.
sequence: Take a paragraph on street trees and ask what its one claim is.
Write the claim as a topic sentence.
Show a sentence that belongs to a different claim.
Reorder sentences from general to specific.
End with a link to the next claim.
examples: A paragraph claims that trees lower street temperature, supported by two measurements and an explanation. A sentence about the cost of planting belongs in a different paragraph.

figures.shows: The passage model with a paragraph's sentences as lines; the off-topic line is not marked.
figures.learnerAction: Select the sentence that does not belong.

questionPlan.sample: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about temperature measurements?
questionPlan.answer: Shaded streets measured several degrees cooler than unshaded ones
choices: Shaded streets measured several degrees cooler than unshaded ones

questionPlan.sample: In a paragraph on temperature, a sentence about planting costs:
questionPlan.answer: Belongs in a different paragraph

questionPlan.sample: A topic sentence is best when it:
questionPlan.answer: States a claim the rest of the paragraph supports
choices: States a claim the rest of the paragraph supports

lessons.title: Evidence and what you say about it
lessons.objective: Choose evidence for a claim, introduce and explain it, and report a percentage correctly.

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.summary: Data, a quotation, an example or an authority that supports a claim.

concepts.title: Analysis
concepts.summary: The writer's explanation of what the evidence shows and why it supports the claim.

concepts.title: Signal phrase
concepts.summary: A phrase that introduces a source, such as 'According to the survey'.

misconceptions: Dropping a quotation into a paragraph without introduction or comment.
Assuming the evidence speaks for itself.
Quoting when a paraphrase would do.
sequence: Show a claim followed by a bare quotation, and ask what the reader is meant to see.
Add an introduction, the evidence and an explanation: lead in, evidence, tie back.
Choose between quoting, paraphrasing and giving a number.
Report a number: 47 of 200 respondents is 23.5%.
Say what the evidence cannot show.
examples: 47 of 200 respondents is 47 / 200 = 0.235, which is 23.5%. A claim, then 'According to the survey, 23.5% of respondents...', then one sentence on why that supports the claim.

figures.shows: A claim, an evidence item and an analysis sentence in three columns, with the analysis blank.
figures.learnerAction: Choose the analysis sentence that ties the evidence to the claim.

questionPlan.sample: 47 of 200 respondents said yes. What percentage is that?
The weakest use of a quotation is:
questionPlan.answer: Dropping it in with no introduction or comment
choices: Dropping it in with no introduction or comment

questionPlan.sample: After a piece of evidence you should:
questionPlan.answer: Say what it shows and how it supports the claim
choices: Say what it shows and how it supports the claim

lessons.title: Answering the other side
lessons.objective: State the strongest objection fairly, reply to it, and qualify a claim to the strength the evidence allows.

concepts.title: Counterargument
concepts.summary: A reason a reasonable reader might give against your thesis.

concepts.title: Concession
concepts.summary: Granting what is right in the objection.

concepts.title: Qualifier
concepts.summary: A word or phrase that limits a claim, such as 'in hot climates' or 'usually'.

misconceptions: Answering a weaker version of the objection that nobody holds.
Believing that any concession weakens the argument.
Qualifying so heavily that no claim remains.
sequence: Show a thesis and ask: what would a sensible critic say?
Write the objection in its strongest form.
Concede what is right, then show why the thesis still holds.
Qualify the claim so that it matches the evidence.
Place the objection where the reader will raise it.
examples: Thesis: cities in hot climates should plant street trees first. Strongest objection: trees need water, which is scarce in hot climates. Concession: that is true. Reply: some species need little water once established, and shade reduces other cooling demands. Qualified claim: in hot, but not water-scarce, climates.

figures.shows: The toulmin model with claim, grounds, qualifier and rebuttal slots; the rebuttal text is hidden.
figures.learnerAction: Pick the rebuttal that best fits the claim.

questionPlan.sample: The strongest form of an objection is the one:
questionPlan.answer: A thoughtful critic would actually make
choices: A thoughtful critic would actually make

questionPlan.sample: Which claim is best qualified?
questionPlan.answer: In hot but water-rich cities, street trees usually lower temperatures
choices: In hot but water-rich cities, street trees usually lower temperatures

questionPlan.sample: In Toulmin's scheme a word like 'usually' that limits a claim is called a what?
questionPlan.answer: qualifier

lessons.title: Openings, endings and transitions
lessons.objective: Choose the connective that matches the relation between two sentences, and write an opening and ending that do work.

concepts.title: Transition
concepts.summary: A word or phrase that tells the reader how a sentence relates to the one before.

concepts.title: Opening
concepts.summary: The move that brings the reader from their world to your question and thesis.

concepts.title: Ending
concepts.summary: The move that says what follows from the argument and not merely what was said.

misconceptions: Using 'however' for any change of subject.
Opening with a broad statement about all of human history.
Ending by repeating the introduction.
sequence: Show two sentences and ask what relation holds between them: contrast, cause, example or addition.
Match the relation to a connective: however, therefore, for instance, moreover.
Show how the join in a sentence can be changed and how that changes the relation.
Write an opening: context, problem, thesis.
Write an ending: what follows, what remains open.
examples: 'Shade lowers temperatures; however, trees need water.' contrast. 'Shade lowers temperatures; therefore cooling demand falls.' cause. 'Some species need little water; for instance, ...' example.

figures.shows: The clauses model with a join between two clauses and the relation hidden; the learner swaps the connective and sees the relation named.
figures.learnerAction: Pick the connective that fits the relation.

questionPlan.sample: 'Shade lowers temperatures; ___ trees need water.' Which connective shows contrast: however or therefore?
questionPlan.answer: however

questionPlan.sample: The connective that shows cause is:
questionPlan.answer: therefore

questionPlan.sample: A good ending of an essay:
questionPlan.answer: Says what follows from the argument
choices: Says what follows from the argument

lessons.title: Revising the whole
lessons.objective: Use a reverse outline to find problems in the structure and order the stages of revision.

concepts.title: Reverse outline
concepts.summary: A list of what each paragraph of a draft actually says, made after the draft.

concepts.title: Global and local revision
concepts.summary: Global revision changes the argument and structure; local revision changes sentences and words.

concepts.title: Revision order
concepts.summary: Revising argument first, then structure, paragraphs, sentences and proofreading.

misconceptions: Starting with commas and word choice.
Revising only what is marked wrong rather than rereading the argument.
Treating the outline as finished before the draft.
sequence: Write one line for each paragraph of a draft: what does it say?
Read the list: does it follow the plan, repeat itself, or jump?
Move, merge, cut or add paragraphs.
Order the stages of revision from largest to smallest.
Stop at the stage where changes no longer improve the piece.
examples: A reverse outline shows paragraphs 3 and 5 both claim that shade lowers temperature: merge them. Revision order: argument, structure, paragraphs, sentences, proofreading.

questionPlan.sample: Order the stages of revision: Proofreading; Sentences; Argument; Paragraphs; Structure.
questionPlan.answer: Argument, Structure, Paragraphs, Sentences, Proofreading

questionPlan.sample: A reverse outline shows two paragraphs making the same point. You should:
questionPlan.answer: Merge or cut one

questionPlan.sample: A reverse outline is made:
questionPlan.answer: After the draft

lessons.title: Clear and short sentences
lessons.objective: Cut a passage by a stated fraction without losing meaning and recast a nominalised sentence.

concepts.title: Nominalisation
concepts.summary: Turning an action into a noun, as in 'make a decision' for 'decide'.

concepts.title: Actors and actions
concepts.summary: A clear sentence puts the actor in the subject and the action in the verb.

concepts.title: Economy
concepts.summary: Using only the words the meaning needs.

misconceptions: Cutting words without checking that every fact is kept.
Believing shorter always means better.
Replacing the actor with a passive and hiding who did the thing.
sequence: Show a wordy sentence and mark what it needs and what it does not.
Rewrite 'make a decision' as 'decide' and 'give consideration to' as 'consider'.
Return actors to the subject.
Cut by a third and check the numbers and names are all still there.
Cite Orwell's rule: if it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out.
examples: A 150-word paragraph cut to 100 words has lost 50 words, or one third (33.3%). A 240-word paragraph cut by one third becomes 160 words. 'The committee made a decision to approve' becomes 'The committee decided to approve'.

figures.shows: The compress model: a sentence in segments marked keep, cut or replace; the verdicts are hidden until the learner chooses.
figures.learnerAction: Mark each segment keep, cut or replace.

questionPlan.sample: A 240-word paragraph is cut by one third. How many words remain?
A 150-word paragraph is cut to 100 words. What percentage was cut, to one decimal place?
'The committee made a decision to approve the plan' is best recast as:
questionPlan.answer: The committee decided to approve the plan
choices: The committee made a decision to approve the plan
The committee decided to approve the plan
A decision was made by the committee

historyNotes: Orwell's rule 'If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out' is from Politics and the English Language (1946); check wording before quoting.

lessons.title: A process that finishes
lessons.objective: Plan a writing schedule backwards from the deadline and use feedback and proofreading effectively.

concepts.title: Backward plan
concepts.summary: A schedule built from the deadline back to the start.

concepts.title: Feedback
concepts.summary: A reader's response to the piece; the most useful kind answers a question you asked.

concepts.title: Proofreading
concepts.summary: A last pass for errors, done after all other revision and on the page or aloud.

misconceptions: Spending all the time on research and none on revision.
Asking a reader 'is it good?'.
Proofreading before revising, which wastes the proofreading.
sequence: Start from a deadline of 14 days and a 3,000-word piece.
Allocate days: research 3, outline 1, draft 4, revise 4, proofread 2.
Compute daily words for the draft: 3,000 / 4 = 750.
Ask a reader specific questions: What is my thesis? Where did you stop following?
Proofread aloud, once, last.
examples: Schedule: 3 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 14 days. Drafting 3,000 words in 4 days is 750 words a day. A reader asked 'Where did you stop following?' gives more than one asked 'Is it good?'.

figures.shows: A 14-day grid with a stage in each block to be placed.
figures.learnerAction: Place the five stages so the days total 14.

questionPlan.sample: Research 3, outline 1, draft 4, revise 4, proofread 2. How many days in total?
Drafting 3,000 words over 4 days is how many words a day?
Rate your recall: name two specific questions you could ask a reader about a draft.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated 1 to 5

lessons.title: The shape of a report
lessons.objective: Organise a report with the answer first, headings that signpost, and a summary that stands alone.

concepts.title: Executive summary
concepts.summary: A short opening section giving the question, finding and recommendation so a reader can act without reading further.

concepts.title: IMRaD
concepts.summary: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion: the usual order of a research report.

concepts.title: Signpost heading
concepts.summary: A heading that says what the section tells the reader, not only its topic.

misconceptions: Burying the recommendation at the end.
Writing headings that name a topic but not a finding.
Copying the research report order for a decision report.
sequence: Compare two reports: one with findings first, one built as a chronicle.
Name the sections of a decision report and a research report.
Write a summary: question, finding, recommendation, cost.
Rewrite a topic heading as a signpost heading.
Check that the summary survives alone.
examples: Decision report: summary and recommendation; background; findings; options; recommendation and next steps. Research report: introduction; methods; results; discussion. Heading: 'Costs' becomes 'Switching suppliers saves 12% in the first year' (an example heading, not a datum).

figures.learnerAction: Order them for a decision report.

questionPlan.sample: Order a decision report: Findings; Summary and recommendation; Options; Background; Next steps.
questionPlan.answer: Summary and recommendation, Background, Findings, Options, Next steps

questionPlan.sample: An executive summary should:
questionPlan.answer: Stand alone and give the finding and recommendation
choices: Stand alone and give the finding and recommendation

questionPlan.sample: What does the I stand for in IMRaD?
questionPlan.answer: Introduction

lessons.title: Numbers, tables and figures
lessons.objective: Compute a percentage change, choose a table or chart, and make a caption and the text agree with the numbers.

concepts.title: Percent change
concepts.summary: (New - old) / old, expressed as a percentage.

concepts.title: Percentage points
concepts.summary: The difference between two percentages, which is not the same as percent change.

concepts.title: Caption
concepts.summary: A line that tells the reader what the figure shows and what to notice.

misconceptions: Reading a rise from 80 to 100 as 20%, when it is 25%.
Confusing percentage points with percent.
Letting the text claim more than the chart shows.
sequence: Compute a change in both directions: 80 to 100 is up 25%, 100 to 80 is down 20%.
Compare percentage points with percent: 10% to 15% is 5 percentage points and a 50% increase.
Choose a display: a line for time, a bar for categories, a table for exact values.
Write a caption that states what to notice.
Check the text against the numbers.

figures.shows: A line of quarterly figures with the text claim beside it; the claim contains one error the learner must find.
figures.learnerAction: Find which statement does not match the data.

questionPlan.sample: Sales rise from 80 to 100. What is the percent change?
Sales fall from 100 to 80. What is the percent change (give the size)?
A rate rises from 10% to 15%. By how many percentage points?

courseCheck: A mixed set: set a word budget; pick the strongest thesis; order sections of an essay and a report; choose topic sentences and spot an off-topic sentence; compute a percentage and recast a nominalisation; qualify a claim and choose a connective; order the stages of revision; cut a paragraph by a fraction; plan a schedule backwards; compute percent change and percentage points.
platformNeeds: draft_review figure: a short draft whose paragraphs the learner can tag (claim, evidence, analysis, transition) with a reverse-outline view. Fallback: table plus language_explorer passage.
word_budget calculator figure: sliders for section shares with a running total. Fallback: table.
Free-text feedback is not marked: any practice of writing a thesis or paragraph is by choice between candidates; a future peer or tutor review mode would let learners practise composition itself.
language_explorer already covers toulmin, compress, clauses with joins, and passage; no new figure type is required.
unverified: Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle as the source of answer first, and its date.
Orwell's rule wording ('If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out') and the 1946 date of Politics and the English Language.
Toulmin's The Uses of Argument as 1958.
The Harvard, UNC and Purdue pages named on George's Notion page: URLs from his page, not opened.
OpenStax Writing Guide with Handbook licence and chapters, from memory.
The example heading 'Switching suppliers saves 12%' and the survey figures are invented for exercises and must be labelled so.
No source was opened (external hosts were blocked); every source is marked verified false.
